courseTitle: Causes of the Great War: Unification to Sarajevo (1862–1914)
eyebrow: Key Stage 3 History • Year 9 Origins of WWI Enquiry

eras.title: Part 1: German Unification, Secret Alliances & Weltpolitik (1862–1900)
Part 2: Moroccan Crises, The Dreadnought Race & Balkan Wars (1904–1913)
Part 3: Sarajevo, The July Crisis & Outbreak of World War (June–August 1914)

milestones.title: Bismarck’s "Blood and Iron" Wars & The Encirclement at Sedan
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Bismarck’s "Blood and Iron" policy make Prussia dominant?
milestones.imageCaption: Wilhelm Camphausen, Napoleon III Captured After Sedan (2 September 1870, Deutsches Historisches Museum): Bismarck meets the defeated French Emperor after Prussian encirclement.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Prussian expansion, the 1870–71 Franco-Prussian War, and German Unification in Central Europe.
milestones.catalyst: With Central Europe split into **39 German states**, Prussian Minister-President **Otto von Bismarck** declared in **1862** that great questions are decided by **"Blood and Iron"**, defeating Denmark (1864) and Austria (1866).
milestones.turningPoint: Armed with **Krupp breech-loading steel cannon** and rapid military railways, Prussian armies encircled France at **Sedan on 2 September 1870**, capturing **Emperor Napoleon III** and over 80,000 troops.
milestones.impact: Toppled France’s Second Empire and rallied independent southern German kingdoms behind Prussian leadership.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Four months later inside occupied France, German princes proclaimed a new **continental superpower** in the Palace of **Versailles**.

keyTerms.definition: Bismarck’s ruthless, practical statecraft grounded in industrial strength and military force rather than moral idealism.
Prussian-led customs union formed in 1834 that integrated German economies while excluding rival Austria.

milestones.title: Crowning the Kaiser at Versailles & The Punitive Treaty of Frankfurt
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the 1871 Treaty of Frankfurt create bitter hatred in France?
milestones.imageCaption: Anton von Werner, Proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles (18 January 1871): Wilhelm I is acclaimed Kaiser in the Hall of Mirrors with Bismarck in white uniform.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The newly unified German Empire and the annexed coal-and-iron provinces of Alsace-Lorraine (May 1871).
milestones.catalyst: On **18 January 1871**, German princes gathered inside Louis XIV’s **Hall of Mirrors at Versailles** to crown Prussian King Wilhelm I as **German Emperor (Kaiser)**.
milestones.turningPoint: Under the **10 May 1871 Treaty of Frankfurt**, Bismarck imposed a **5 billion gold franc indemnity** and annexed France’s iron-and-coal borderlands of **Alsace-Lorraine**.
milestones.impact: Overturned Europe’s balance of power overnight while inflicting a permanent territorial wound that made **France** an implacable enemy on Germany’s western border.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Dreading a future **two-front war**, Bismarck moved between **1879 and 1882** to lock Central Europe into a defensive military bloc.

keyTerms.definition: Coal- and iron-rich eastern French provinces annexed by Germany under the May 1871 Treaty of Frankfurt.
Deep-seated French national determination for vengeance against Germany and recovery of Alsace-Lorraine.

milestones.title: The 1879 Dual Alliance & 1882 Triple Alliance in Central Europe
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy form the Triple Alliance?
milestones.imageCaption: Chancellor Otto von Bismarck (portrait by Franz von Lenbach): Architect of the 1879 Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary and the 1882 Triple Alliance with Italy.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The Central European Triple Alliance bloc (Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy) formed between 1879 and 1882.
milestones.catalyst: Bismarck feared that humiliated **France** might one day join **Tsarist Russia** to crush Germany simultaneously from west and east.
milestones.turningPoint: Germany signed the secret **1879 Dual Alliance** promising mutual defence with **Austria-Hungary** against Russian attack, expanding in **1882** when **Italy** joined to form the **Triple Alliance**.
milestones.impact: Created a powerful Central European military coalition stretching from the Baltic to the Mediterranean, alarming both Paris and St Petersburg.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Two years later, Bismarck hosted fourteen powers at the **1884–1885 Berlin Conference** as imperial competition surged across **Africa**.

keyTerms.definition: Defensive military pact formed in 1882 uniting Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy against rival Great Powers.
Historians’ framework of Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, and Nationalism driving pre-1914 European tension.

milestones.title: The Berlin Conference & Colonial Rivalry in the Scramble for Africa
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did colonial rivalry in Africa and Kaiser Wilhelm’s ambitions fuel tension?
milestones.imageCaption: Adalbert von Roessler, The Berlin Conference (1884–1885): Bismarck and European ambassadors establishing "effective occupation" rules over a wall map of Africa.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Imperial partition of Africa after the 1884–1885 Berlin Conference.
milestones.catalyst: Industrialising European powers raced across Africa to seize **rubber, copper, palm oil, and captive markets**, risking accidental colonial clashes.
milestones.turningPoint: At the **1884–1885 Berlin Conference**, fourteen powers agreed on **"effective occupation"**, triggering an inland stampede in which **Britain and France** secured the richest empires.
milestones.impact: Left late-unified **Germany** holding smaller colonial territories, planting seeds of imperial envy among German nationalists.
milestones.bridgeToNext: While French schools preached **revanche**, Bismarck signed one final secret pact in **June 1887** to stop Russia allying with France.

keyTerms.definition: Germany’s later global colonial policy fuelled by resentment over Britain and France’s larger overseas empires.
Bismarck’s calculated use of colonial conferences in Berlin to deflect European rivalries away from Germany’s borders.

milestones.title: French Schoolroom Revanche & Bismarck’s 1887 Reinsurance Treaty
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Bismarck’s 1887 treaty with Russia keep France isolated?
milestones.imageCaption: Albert Bettannier, La Tache Noire ("The Black Spot", 1887): A French teacher points cadet-uniformed pupils toward blacked-out Alsace-Lorraine.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Bismarck’s diplomatic web isolating France between 1871 and 1890.
milestones.catalyst: Across the French Third Republic, conscription and classroom maps veiled in black crepe kept **revanche** for **Alsace-Lorraine** burning across a new generation.
milestones.turningPoint: On **18 June 1887**, Bismarck signed the secret **Reinsurance Treaty** with **Tsarist Russia**, pledging mutual neutrality unless Germany attacked France or Russia attacked Austria.
milestones.impact: Prevented a Franco-Russian encirclement and preserved fragile European peace—so long as Berlin renewed its Russian tie.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Everything changed in **1889–1890**: Britain codified naval supremacy just as **Kaiser Wilhelm II** sacked Bismarck and abandoned Russia.

keyTerms.definition: Secret June 1887 pact between Germany and Russia pledging neutrality to prevent a two-front Franco-Russian alliance.
Patriotic French movement mourning the "lost provinces" of Alsace-Lorraine and preparing youth for future recovery.

milestones.title: Britain’s 1889 Two-Power Standard & Wilhelm II’s 1890 Weltpolitik
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Kaiser Wilhelm II sack Bismarck and launch Weltpolitik in 1890?
milestones.imageCaption: HMS Majestic at the Spithead Fleet Review (Charles Dixon, 1897): Importing over 60% of its food by sea, island Britain enforced the 1889 Two-Power Standard.
milestones.mapCaption: Walter Crane, Imperial Federation Map of the World (1886), illustrating the global sea lanes Britain’s Two-Power Standard guarded.
milestones.catalyst: Importing **over 60% of its food by sea**, island Britain passed the **1889 Naval Defence Act**, requiring the Royal Navy to match the next two largest fleets combined.
milestones.turningPoint: In **March 1890**, twenty-nine-year-old **Kaiser Wilhelm II** dismissed **Bismarck**, let the Russian **Reinsurance Treaty** lapse, and launched **Weltpolitik** demanding Germany’s **"place in the sun"**.
milestones.impact: Shattered Bismarck’s cautious balance of power: isolated Russia looked westward to Paris while Wilhelm craved an ocean battlefleet.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Within four years (**1894**), French gold sealed the **Franco-Russian Alliance**, while **Admiral von Tirpitz** launched Germany’s naval challenge (**1898–1900**).

keyTerms.definition: Statutory 1889 British naval rule requiring the Royal Navy to equal at least the next two largest foreign fleets combined.
Kaiser Wilhelm II’s aggressive post-1890 "World Policy" pursuing overseas colonies and a global German battlefleet.

milestones.title: The 1894 Franco-Russian Alliance & Tirpitz’s "Risk Theory" Fleet
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Admiral von Tirpitz’s 1898 "Risk Theory" threaten Britain?
milestones.imageCaption: German Battleship SMS Nassau of the High Seas Fleet (U.S. Naval History NH 46827): Built under Admiral von Tirpitz’s Naval Laws directly across the North Sea.
milestones.catalyst: After Wilhelm dropped the Russian treaty, French loans financed Russian strategic railways, sealing the **1894 Franco-Russian Military Alliance** on both German borders.
milestones.turningPoint: In **1898 and 1900**, Naval Secretary **Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz** steered **German Naval Laws** through the Reichstag to build a powerful North Sea fleet under **"Risk Theory"** (*Risikotheorie*).
milestones.impact: Instead of scaring Britain into neutrality, concentrating German battleships hours from England convinced London that Germany threatened British survival.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Naval alarm pushed Britain to end "Splendid Isolation" via the **1904 Entente Cordiale**—immediately tested by Wilhelm at **Tangier in March 1905**.

keyTerms.definition: Tirpitz’s calculation that a strong German North Sea fleet would deter Britain from risking costly battle against Germany.
Reichstag statutes of 1898 and 1900 authorizing massive long-term expansion of Germany’s High Seas Fleet.

milestones.title: The 1904 Entente Cordiale & Kaiser Wilhelm’s Landing at Tangier
milestones.specTag: First Moroccan Crisis Tests Anglo-French Pact
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Kaiser Wilhelm II ride into Tangier on a white horse in 1905?
milestones.imageCaption: Kaiser Wilhelm II Rides Through Tangier (31 March 1905): Publicly backing Moroccan independence on a white horse to split the new 1904 Anglo-French Entente Cordiale.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Tangier (March 1905) and Algeciras (1906) during the First Moroccan Crisis.
milestones.catalyst: Alarmed by German naval growth, Britain and France settled colonial disputes in Egypt and Morocco under the **April 1904 Entente Cordiale**.
milestones.turningPoint: On **31 March 1905**, **Kaiser Wilhelm II** landed dramatically at **Tangier**, rode a white horse to the German legation, and saluted the Sultan of **Morocco** as an independent sovereign.
milestones.impact: Designed to humiliate France and expose Britain as an unreliable friend, Wilhelm’s provocation plunged Europe into the **First Moroccan Crisis**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Berlin demanded an international summit at **Algeciras in early 1906**, confident Britain would abandon France—a disastrous miscalculation.

keyTerms.definition: April 1904 Anglo-French agreement resolving colonial disputes in Egypt and Morocco and launching close diplomatic cooperation.
Using theatrical naval visits and military intimidation to extract diplomatic concessions from rival powers.

milestones.title: German Isolation at Algeciras & Secret Anglo-French Staff Talks
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the 1906 Algeciras Conference backfire on German diplomacy?
milestones.imageCaption: Bernard Partridge, Punch cartoon celebrating Anglo-French solidarity: German pressure at Algeciras (1906) turned the Entente Cordiale into joint military planning.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Diplomatic isolation of Germany at the 1906 Algeciras Conference in southern Spain.
milestones.catalyst: Germany forced France to attend the **January–April 1906 Algeciras Conference** in Spain to debate policing and banking control over Morocco.
milestones.turningPoint: Britain, Russia, and even Germany’s nominal ally Italy backed France, leaving Berlin humiliated **12 votes to 2**—supported only by **Austria-Hungary**.
milestones.impact: Instead of breaking the Entente, German bullying prompted **Britain and France** to begin **secret joint military staff talks** in London.
milestones.bridgeToNext: That same winter of **February 1906**, Britain unveiled a revolutionary battleship at Portsmouth while moving to settle differences with **Russia (1907)**.

keyTerms.definition: 1906 international summit in Spain where twelve nations backed France in Morocco, leaving Germany diplomatically isolated.
Anglo-French alignment strengthened into secret military planning as a direct result of Germany’s 1905–1906 Moroccan pressure.

milestones.title: HMS Dreadnought Resets the Naval Race & The 1907 Triple Entente
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did launching HMS Dreadnought in 1906 wipe out Britain’s lead?
milestones.imageCaption: HMS Dreadnought at Sea (1906): Armed with ten 12-inch guns and steam turbines, Jackie Fisher’s battleship rendered every older pre-dreadnought obsolete overnight.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Completion of the Triple Entente (Britain, France, and Russia, 1907) facing the Central Triple Alliance.
milestones.catalyst: Determined to outclass Tirpitz’s fleet, First Sea Lord **Admiral Sir John "Jackie" Fisher** launched **HMS Dreadnought** in **February 1906** with **ten 12-inch guns** and fast steam turbines.
milestones.turningPoint: Because *Dreadnought* made all older battleships **instantly obsolete**, Britain’s huge lead in older warships vanished—letting Germany race almost from scratch—while the **August 1907 Anglo-Russian Entente** completed the **Triple Entente**.
milestones.impact: Locked Europe into **two armed alliance blocs** while igniting a furious Anglo-German dreadnought construction race across the North Sea.
milestones.bridgeToNext: With rival alliances hardened, attention swung in **October 1908** to Europe’s volatile **"Balkan Powder Keg"**.

keyTerms.definition: Revolutionary 1906 British turbine-powered, all-big-gun battleship class that reset global naval competition.
Diplomatic alignment of Great Britain, France, and Russia completed in August 1907.

milestones.title: Austria Annexes Bosnia-Herzegovina & Humiliates Russia
milestones.specTag: Pan-Slav Outrage in the Balkan Powder Keg
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Austria’s 1908 seizure of Bosnia anger Serbia and Russia?
milestones.imageCaption: The Bosnian Annexation Crisis (Le Petit Journal, 18 October 1908): Emperor Franz Joseph seizing Bosnia-Herzegovina outraged Serbia and humiliated Tsarist Russia.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Bosnia-Herzegovina annexed by Austria-Hungary (October 1908) beside independent Serbia.
milestones.catalyst: As Ottoman rule crumbled across south-eastern Europe, independent **Serbia** hoped to unite South Slavs—including Slavic **Bosnia-Herzegovina**—under **Pan-Slavism**.
milestones.turningPoint: In **October 1908**, **Austria-Hungary** unilaterally annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina; when **Russia** protested in support of furious Serbia, **Germany** backed Vienna and forced militarily unready Russia to back down.
milestones.impact: Serbian nationalists formed underground groups like the **Black Hand**, while humiliated **Tsar Nicholas II** vowed Russia would **never yield to Austro-German threats again**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Months later in **1909**, fears of secret German shipyard acceleration triggered nationwide **naval panic** across Great Britain.

keyTerms.definition: South-eastern Europe, where Ottoman decline, Slavic nationalism, and Austro-Russian rivalry threatened continental war.
Unilateral seizure of territory—such as Austria-Hungary’s October 1908 takeover of Bosnia-Herzegovina.
Nationalist movement seeking to unite Slavic peoples in the Balkans with Tsarist Russia as their protector.

milestones.title: "We Want Eight and We Won’t Wait!" — The 1909 Dreadnought Panic
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did British crowds chant "We want eight and we won’t wait" in 1909?
milestones.imageCaption: Launch of Dreadnought Battleship HMS Neptune at Portsmouth (30 September 1909): Amid the 1909 Naval Panic, Britain funded eight dreadnoughts in a single year.
milestones.catalyst: Admiralty intelligence warned in **1909** that German Krupp yards were stockpiling heavy guns and secretly accelerating dreadnought construction.
milestones.turningPoint: Sensational headlines and marching crowds chanted **"We want eight and we won’t wait!"**, compelling Britain’s Liberal Cabinet to fund **eight new dreadnoughts** in a single budget.
milestones.impact: Ensured Britain kept a 29-to-17 dreadnought lead by 1914, yet poisoned public opinion in both countries with mutual invasion fear.
milestones.bridgeToNext: In **July 1911**, Kaiser Wilhelm’s dispatch of a German gunboat to **Agadir** brought Britain and Germany to the brink of war.

keyTerms.definition: Capital warship at the centre of the 1909 British public campaign demanding eight new battleships in one year.
Maritime benchmark driving British determination never to let Tirpitz’s High Seas Fleet close the dreadnought gap.

milestones.title: The Gunboat SMS Panther at Agadir & Lloyd George’s Warning
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did sending the gunboat Panther to Agadir in 1911 alarm Britain?
milestones.imageCaption: German Gunboat SMS Panther (July 1911): Sent to the Moroccan Atlantic port of Agadir, provoking David Lloyd George’s stern Mansion House warning.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Agadir on Morocco’s Atlantic coast (July 1911), directly threatening British sea routes.
milestones.catalyst: When French troops entered Fez in **1911**, Berlin dispatched the gunboat **SMS Panther** to the Atlantic port of **Agadir** to demand the French Congo as compensation.
milestones.turningPoint: Fearing a German Atlantic naval base, British Chancellor **David Lloyd George** warned in his **21 July 1911 Mansion House speech** that Britain would fight rather than see peace preserved by humiliation.
milestones.impact: Forced Germany to back down for minor Congo strips, deepening Berlin’s paranoia of "encirclement" while Britain and France coordinated naval war zones.
milestones.bridgeToNext: In **1912–1913**, Berlin naval talks collapsed just as **two Balkan Wars** doubled **Serbia’s** size on Austria-Hungary’s doorstep.

keyTerms.definition: 21 July 1911 speech by British Chancellor David Lloyd George warning Germany that Britain would stand by France.
Germany’s dispatch of SMS Panther to Agadir in July 1911 to coerce colonial concessions from France.

milestones.title: Failure of the Haldane Mission & Serbia Triumphant in the Balkan Wars
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Serbia’s victories in the 1912–1913 Balkan Wars alarm Vienna?
milestones.imageCaption: Serbian Infantry in Action During the First Balkan War (1912): Victory in 1912–1913 doubled Serbia’s territory and army strength.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Expanded post-1913 Serbia and the volatile Balkan frontier with Austria-Hungary.
milestones.catalyst: Lord Haldane’s **February 1912** Berlin naval truce talks failed when Germany demanded unconditional British neutrality, prompting Britain to concentrate battleships in the **North Sea** and **Moltke** to call war "inevitable" (Dec 1912).
milestones.turningPoint: Meanwhile in the **1912–1913 Balkan Wars**, the Balkan League drove Ottoman rule almost out of Europe and **Serbia doubled its land** and fielded **400,000 battle-hardened troops**.
milestones.impact: Terrified that victorious Serbia would inspire Slavic breakaways inside Austria-Hungary, hawkish generals in **Vienna** resolved to **crush Serbia** at the next crisis.
milestones.bridgeToNext: That fatal spark arrived on **28 June 1914** when **Archduke Franz Ferdinand** visited the Bosnian capital of **Sarajevo**.

keyTerms.definition: Failed February 1912 British diplomatic mission to Berlin seeking an Anglo-German dreadnought building holiday.
Region brought to boiling point by 1913 as victorious Serbia confronted an anxious Austro-Hungarian Empire.

milestones.title: Two Shots at the Latin Bridge: Gavrilo Princip Kills Franz Ferdinand
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Gavrilo Princip assassinate Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo?
milestones.imageCaption: Archduke Franz Ferdinand & Duchess Sophie Leaving Sarajevo Town Hall (28 June 1914, Walter Tausch): Minutes before their car turned in front of Gavrilo Princip.
milestones.mapCaption: Austro-Hungarian Police Map of the Appel Quay Motorcade Route and Fatal Wrong Turn at the Latin Bridge, Sarajevo (28 June 1914).
milestones.catalyst: Heir to the Habsburg throne **Archduke Franz Ferdinand** toured annexed **Sarajevo** with his wife Sophie on **28 June 1914**, narrowly surviving a morning Black Hand grenade on the Appel Quay.
milestones.turningPoint: Minutes later, the royal chauffeur took a **wrong turn** into Franz Josef Street and halted directly beside nineteen-year-old Bosnian-Serb nationalist **Gavrilo Princip**, who **fired two fatal shots**.
milestones.impact: Handed Austro-Hungarian military hawks the exact pretext they wanted to destroy independent **Serbia**—provided Berlin guaranteed protection against Russia.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Seven days later in Berlin (**5 July 1914**), **Kaiser Wilhelm II** handed Vienna an unconditional military guarantee.

keyTerms.definition: Secret Serbian nationalist society that armed Young Bosnia conspirators including Gavrilo Princip.
Austria’s 1908 seizure of Bosnia that fuelled underground student resistance culminating at Sarajevo in June 1914.

milestones.title: Germany’s "Blank Cheque", The 10-Point Ultimatum & Shelling of Belgrade
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Kaiser’s 5 July "blank cheque" embolden Austria-Hungary?
milestones.imageCaption: Emperor Franz Joseph I and Kaiser Wilhelm II: On 5 July 1914 Berlin issued its unconditional "Blank Cheque", emboldening Vienna to attack Serbia.
milestones.mapCaption: Causal Flowchart of the July Crisis (28 June – 4 August 1914), from Sarajevo and the Blank Cheque to general war.
milestones.catalyst: Fearing Russian intervention if Austria invaded Serbia, Vienna sent envoys to Berlin seeking Kaiser Wilhelm II’s backing.
milestones.turningPoint: Armed with Germany’s unconditional **5 July "Blank Cheque"**, Austria issued a harsh **48-hour, ten-point ultimatum** (23 July)—demanding Austrian police operate inside Belgrade—and **declared war on 28 July** despite Serbia accepting nine terms.
milestones.impact: Austrian gunboats shelled Belgrade across the Danube on **28 July 1914**, turning a diplomatic dispute into active Balkan warfare.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Refusing a second 1908 humiliation, **Tsar Nicholas II** ordered **general Russian mobilisation**, triggering rigid railway timetables across Europe.

keyTerms.definition: Kaiser Wilhelm II’s 5 July 1914 pledge of unconditional German military support for whatever action Austria took against Serbia.
Austria-Hungary’s non-negotiable 23 July ten-point demand drafted deliberately so sovereign Serbia could not accept every clause.

milestones.title: Russian Mobilisation, The Schlieffen Invasion of Belgium & British Entry
milestones.specTag: "Scrap of Paper" Brings Britain Into War
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Germany’s invasion of Belgium bring Britain into the war?
milestones.imageCaption: F. H. Townsend, "Bravo, Belgium!" (Punch, 12 August 1914): Germany’s 4 August invasion of neutral Belgium brought Great Britain into the First World War by midnight.
milestones.mapCaption: West Point Strategic Map of the Schlieffen Plan: German 1st–5th Armies wheeling through neutral Belgium toward Paris (August 1914).
milestones.catalyst: **Tsar Nicholas II’s 30 July** general mobilisation activated rigid **railway timetables**; Germany declared war on Russia (1 August) and France (3 August) to execute the **Schlieffen Plan**.
milestones.turningPoint: Dismissing the **1839 Treaty of London** protecting **Belgian neutrality** as a mere **"scrap of paper"**, German armies invaded Belgium on **4 August 1914** to knock out France inside 42 days.
milestones.impact: When Berlin ignored London’s ultimatum to withdraw, **Great Britain and its Empire entered the war at midnight on 4 August**—thirty-seven days after Sarajevo.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Historians still fiercely debate whether Europe’s leaders **"sleepwalked"** into 1914 or whether Berlin deliberately engineered continental war.

keyTerms.definition: Rapid call-up of millions of reservists onto scheduled military trains that generals claimed could not be halted.
German war plan to defeat France rapidly by sweeping through neutral Belgium before turning east to fight Russia.

milestones.title: Why War Broke Out in 1914: Fritz Fischer vs Christopher Clark
milestones.specTag: Planned German War vs Shared Sleepwalking
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did war break out in 1914?
milestones.imageCaption: Nelson Harding, "The Chain of Friendship" (Brooklyn Daily Eagle, July 1914): Illustrating how interlocking alliances turned a Balkan clash into continental war.
milestones.mapCaption: Analytical Synthesis Diagram: How Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, and Nationalism converged in July–August 1914.
milestones.catalyst: Four decades of **Nationalism** (1871 Alsace-Lorraine & Balkan Pan-Slavism), **Imperialism** (Morocco), **Militarism** (Dreadnoughts & Schlieffen timetables), and **Alliances** piled dry fuel across Europe.
milestones.turningPoint: **Fritz Fischer (1961)** argued Berlin deliberately engineered war—pointing to the **December 1912 War Council** and **Blank Cheque**—whereas **Christopher Clark (2012)** portrayed all Great Powers as **"Sleepwalkers"** blind to catastrophe.
milestones.impact: Understanding **both long-term M-A-I-N structures and July 1914 agency** equips historians to explain why one shooting in Sarajevo unleashed a four-year global conflict.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Completes Part 1’s chronological spine from 1862 Prussian steel to midnight on 4 August 1914—setting the stage for trench warfare in Part 2.

keyTerms.definition: The four interwoven long-term structural causes of 1914: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, and Nationalism.
Central piece of evidence in debates between Fritz Fischer (deliberate German aggression) and Christopher Clark (multilateral miscalculation).
Point, Evidence, Explain, Link—analytical structure connecting long-term tensions to the July 1914 outbreak.
